name: Rafael Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What happened at work this morning?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A wholesaler had paid for a shipment twice, so I spent the morning matching the freight invoice with its bank lines before I touched the tax return. I'm 43, a mid-level accountant at Dockside Tax, experienced but fairly ordinary at the job, with a bachelor's degree and a professional accountancy qualification. I like finding a clean explanation for a client; I dislike another Friday spent asking why a packing slip is missing.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What about the family budget and the tools you use?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Mei is a lab technician, and our children, eight and twelve, know the mortgage envelope stays on the kitchen shelf. My salary is typical for an accountant here, we have four months of expenses saved, and there are some similar firms nearby. I use AI now and then for a first letter after a colleague has tested it, but I compare every invoice number myself. I want a price and a working example before I change a routine, whether the idea comes from a boss or a public office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau — Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell clients a little invoice sorting is useful if the person signing the return still checks the source. I wouldn't promise a shorter bill until the saved time is measured.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our two wages and four months saved make the mortgage feel manageable, and the firm has regular wholesaler work. A bad invoice can still cost a client, but I don't expect my hours to move in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep reconciling freight invoices to bank lines and using AI only for drafts I can verify. In the first year I'd continue putting eighty a month into our mortgage reserve from pay, without changing the children's music budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about income. It would be nice to get one Friday evening back, but I am not counting on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you measure before promising a shorter bill?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How many duplicate freight payments the sorter catches and how long a person spends correcting its misses. If the invoice sorter saves twenty minutes but adds a wrong tax entry, it has not saved the client anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep the music budget?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The children use it every week, and our wages cover it today. I'd change it only if the mortgage reserve began to fall.

say: I would keep a **source check** behind sorted invoices.
I would measure **real time saved** before changing client fees.
think: Our **two wages** and four-month reserve support the mortgage.
I do not expect my **paid hours** to change in a plateau.
do: Keep matching **freight invoices** to bank entries and verifying AI drafts.
Save **eighty monthly** from pay into the mortgage reserve.
feel: He feels **calm** about steady wages and manageable mortgage payments.
S0.quote: If the invoice sorter saves twenty minutes but adds a wrong tax entry, it has not saved the client anything.
fieldNote: He treats a modest sorter as a **measurable cost question**, not a cause for alarm.
The children’s music stays because **current wages** and a four-month reserve support it.

steps.text: Keep matching freight invoices to bank entries and verifying AI drafts
Add eighty monthly from pay to mortgage reserve

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption — Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the partners which checks software takes and which person still signs the file. The team needs a timetable for any change in hours, not a vague promise of efficiency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Checking invoices, writing letters and answering clients take up most of my paid day. I think Dockside will cut a reviewer day across the team, and my own hours could be the ones reduced despite four months saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd test the approved tool on ten closed freight files during a paid afternoon if the partners agree, and compare its missed duplicates with our current method. In the first year of steady change, if my paid week drops below four days, I'd apply for posted accounts posts at the two firms on the train line while keeping Dockside hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about my own hours, though we have a buffer. Four months is enough to search, but it is not a second salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need from a new firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A written offer with the wage, start date and hours, high enough after train fare to keep the mortgage current. Mei can collect the younger child only if her lab shift ends before school does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the partners refuse the trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep checking invoices the current way and ask for a written hours plan. I would not use an unapproved system on a live wholesaler return.

say: I would ask for a **written hours timetable** before software changes reviews.
I would keep a **named signer** on each return.
think: My **checking work** is exposed to strong AI.
My **own hours** could be cut despite four months saved.
do: Test **ten closed freight files** on paid time if approved.
Keep **current invoice checks** if the trial is refused.
Seek **posted train-line accounts** below four paid days, retaining Dockside hours; require written mortgage-covering net pay, start date and confirmed pickup.
feel: He feels **anxious** about a realistic cut to his own hours.
S1.quote: Four months is enough to search, but it is not a second salary.
fieldNote: His paid test compares **missed duplicate payments**, not just faster typing.
A move needs a **written wage** and start date plus pickup coverage after Mei’s lab shift.

steps.text: Test approved AI on ten closed freight files during paid afternoon if partners agree
Keep current freight invoice checking if paid trial refused
Apply for posted train-line accounts below four paid days while keeping Dockside hours
Require written wage/hours/start covering mortgage after train fares and pickup after Mei’s confirmed lab finish

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028 — Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team full AGI in 2028 can prepare the tax and accounts work we sell, so the partners should show us a real staffing plan. I would not say a human will review every return unless the hours are funded.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My desk work faces 2028 directly, while robots around 2031 could reach some of Mei's lab tasks later. I expect Dockside to cut at least one accounting post, and my typical wage could be the one our household loses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd stop our planned kitchen refit and put its two hundred monthly payment into the emergency account. In the first year after 2028, if my post ends, I'd apply for advertised salaried accounts-control roles at the nearby wholesalers and keep any paid Dockside work while waiting for a written offer with wage and start date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed about losing a whole wage. Four months saved cannot carry four people through a long search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move far for one of those roles?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after Mei and I see a written wage that covers the mortgage and the extra commute. The children would stay in their school unless the start date and her lab hours make a move workable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the wholesalers have no vacancies?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Dockside for any paid bank-reconciliation hours it still has and use the reserve for bills. I would not invent a vacancy because a wholesaler has a busy yard.

say: I would demand a **staffing plan** before 2028.
I would ask which **human review hours** clients still fund.
think: My **desk wage** could go when AGI arrives in 2028.
Mei’s **lab tasks** may face robots around 2031.
do: Redirect **two hundred monthly** from the cancelled kitchen refit into cash.
Seek **posted wholesaler accounts** after 2028 job loss, requiring written start and mortgage-covering wage after extra commute costs.
Keep **paid bank-reconciliation hours** if no wholesaler vacancy appears.
feel: He feels **alarmed** about losing a full household wage.
S2.quote: Four months saved cannot carry four people through a long search.
fieldNote: His kitchen decision creates **new liquid savings** rather than relabelling an existing reserve.
He knows a busy wholesaler is **not a posted job**, so he keeps paid firm work until a real written offer.

steps.text: Cancel kitchen refit and add two hundred monthly to emergency cash
Seek posted wholesaler accounts after job loss with written start and mortgage-covering pay after commute
Keep paid Dockside reconciliation work if no wholesaler vacancy is posted

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031 — Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years lets us learn which wholesaler accounts still need a person and price that work honestly. I would want the partners to try it without promising every old post survives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 in 2031 I'd still have a mortgage and children at school. AGI could do freight account checks quickly, and robots around 2034 might change lab work for Mei, so both pay cheques matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the partners next spring for one paid day a month visiting a wholesaler to explain double payments and late invoices, with fees going to Dockside. In the first year after 2031, if the clients renew at a price covering my hours, I'd stay on the salaried visits; if not, I'd apply for posted finance posts at the wholesalers while keeping funded firm hours until a written offer starts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, though a few years let me test a price before the accounts fees fall. I would rather hear a client say no early than guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How many clients would tell you enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start with four and need three to pay for a second visit at a fee covering staff time. If only one renews, the service is a cost, not a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the partners will not fund your visits?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on ordinary returns and ask for a written hours plan. I would not do evening visits for free to prove an idea.

say: I would test **paid wholesaler visits** through Dockside before treating a client meeting as a new wage.
I would require **three renewals** at staff-covering fees.
think: At **48 in 2031**, I still need mortgage wages.
Mei’s **2034 robot risk** could affect lab income later.
do: Pilot **four paid visits** with partner approval next spring.
Continue after **2031** only if three clients renew at covering fees.
Apply for **posted wholesaler finance** work if the visit fees fail.
feel: He feels **anxious**, but can test paid demand before fees fall.
S3.quote: I would rather hear a client say no early than guess.
fieldNote: The service is **firm-owned and salaried**, with a three-client renewal threshold.
A funding refusal means **ordinary paid returns**, not unpaid visits, while a job move needs a posted offer.

steps.text: Pilot four paid wholesaler visits with partner approval and firm fees
Continue salaried visits after 2031 only if three clients renew at covering fees
Seek posted wholesaler finance if visits fail; keep funded firm hours until written offer starts
Keep ordinary paid returns and request written hours plan if partners refuse visit funding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036 — Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade gives families time to reduce debt and firms time to prove which advice still earns a fee. I don't think anyone can promise the exact number of accounting jobs in 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 in 2036 our mortgage might be smaller, but I would still need a wage. AGI reaches my accounts desk then; robots around 2039 could affect Mei's lab work later, so I would not spend all our savings before either date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd add one hundred a month to mortgage principal while both wages hold and keep a record of repeat fees from the wholesaler visits. In the first year after 2036, if those visits still fund my salary, I'd stay; if they do not, I'd apply for posted salaried logistics-office roles and keep any paid Dockside hours until a written wage and start date are agreed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy, not calm, about a mortgage at 53. Ten years can help, but it cannot guarantee a vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Mei loses hours before then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the extra principal payment and hold cash for bills. A smaller loan is useful only if the kitchen still has food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use your savings to buy an AI system?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the firm should pay for tools it wants and test them on its own books. Our four-month reserve is for the children and the loan.

I would use the decade to **reduce mortgage principal**.

Mei’s **2039 robot exposure** could affect lab income.

Track **repeat wholesaler fees** while keeping current paid work.

S4.quote: Ten years can help, but it cannot guarantee a vacancy.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because a whole wage could go while the mortgage and school costs continue. A real staffing plan and posted wholesaler job with a written wage would help. I can compare invoices for hours; I cannot make a job posting appear by staring at a loading yard.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who checks the first tax return after the software makes a mistake. A wrong freight invoice can hide in a very tidy-looking list.

headlineQuote: A wrong freight invoice can hide in a very tidy-looking list.
portrait: Rafael, **43**, is an experienced average-skilled accountant at Dockside Tax with a bachelor’s degree and professional qualification.
His **typical pay**, four-month reserve and Mei’s lab wage support two school-age children and a mortgage.
He uses AI **occasionally after colleagues** test it, while some accounting firms remain reachable by train.
He fears a **2028 post cut** and tests paid wholesaler visits before relying on their fees.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove a whole wage while mortgage and school costs continue.
whatWouldHelp: A **real staffing plan** and posted wholesaler job with written wages would help.
